turn_text: On this episode of the Wise Council Project, we conclude our interview with Georgia Governor Nathan Deal. Join us as Governor Deal provides Wise Council to men and women of faith. Just attended an all-pro dad's conference where Coach Tony Dungee was there, talking to fathers about having them step up to be the leaders in the household. What do you think we can do in Georgia to encourage the dads to be there so we can prevent the kids from going into the juvenile justice system to start with?

Well, that is one of those problems that has been a huge contributor to drop out rates in our high schools and to increases in certain categories in our prison population is that they have not had a father figure in the home. And for young boys in particular, that sometimes poses a great threat to their future. To get fathers involved is not only the right thing to do, but it pays benefits for the entire family unit. And I appreciate what Tony Dungy and others are doing to try to increase that participation rate by fathers in their children's lives, not just boys, but girls as well. children need father figures and sometimes that is the missing element. As we see the number of outer birth wedlocks occurring we see that percentage of absent fathers continue to grow and we need to reverse that trend.

And I know your wife Sandra taught for over 15 years in the public school system, you talked about your parents being teachers. And literacy is an important project that she is the first lady has really been pushing. What other, well we'll talk about literacy first if you would, why you think that's important. I'd love for you to also address what other issues you see facing the young people here in Georgia.

Well, literacy is all important because we know that if a child does not read at third grade level when they leave the third grade, we spend a lot of money, time, effort and tears trying to get them through the graduation lines and many times we're not successful. We believe a focused effort early on to get children interested in reading And making sure that they do read and know how to do it effectively is very, very important. We put an emphasis on it. My wife has taken on the campaign of Read Across Georgia. As a teacher, she knows the importance of this. And she's now read to over 400 different schools in our state and all 159 counties. all 181 school districts. And she continues it every week. She is going and reading to young children. But there are other problems that we're encountering as well. And one of those is the drug problem. I mention to you that we're trying to divert non-violent offenders and juveniles out of our system of either prisons or YDCs. Many of those that are in those categories have substance abuse problems and we're continuing to see the involvement of younger children using drugs at a much earlier age than has historically been the case. Now we're also in seeing an increase in the use of prescription drugs that they're getting out of somebody's medicine cabinet. We've done a pretty good job in tightening up the laws to try to drive out the pill mills that were in our state and I think we have been very effective in doing that. But we're being told by the law enforcement community. that an ever-increasing percentage of people with drug issues are the unauthorized use of prescription drugs. So it takes a focused effort on the part of everybody. Because if a child is getting pain pills out of their parents, a medicine cabinet, then the parent needs to be a little more responsive and be more aware of what's going on. Because those can be just as addictive, if not more addictive, than even illegal drugs. So that's why. That issue is one of the real issues that faces young people and faces family units as well. And please tell me, we're not going to see a push for the legalization of everyone in this state. No, I do not believe that that is a solution. If we want to look at what's happening in Colorado, that is not a model that we need to have in our state.

turn_text: We're talking about issues facing the young people here in Georgia. What other issues are we going to be facing in the state in the next four years?

Well, you know, we've come through some very difficult times. When I became governor, we were still in the midst of the Great Recession. But we have focused on creating jobs for the Georgia citizens, and we've now over around 300,000 private sector jobs since I became governor. That's a huge number. Last year, there were only five other states that were ahead of us in terms of total job creation. Four of the five were states that were two to three times larger in population than we were. So focusing on giving people good jobs I think is a critical element. And I have a little bit of a mantra if you don't mind me saying it with you. An individual who has a good job can support themselves. They can support their family. They can be charitable in their community, and they have less reason to ask government to do things for them. Now I believe that is not only conservatism in action, it is Christianity in action. People need to have the ability to support themselves, and at the core of that is a job.

turn_text: Some advice if I may, and we'll start with, what was the greatest advice that your parents imparted to you?

I suppose the greatest advice was not necessarily verbal advice, but just encouragement. I know that the Bible enumerates various gifts of the Spirit. I think one of the greatest gifts of the Spirit is to be an encourager. That's what parents should be. They should encourage their child as my parents encourage me. Be the best at what you want to be. Explore what your talents lead you to be able to do. And don't be afraid to risk being a failure. The ones who are afraid to take a chance are the ones who never fully reached the potential that God intended them to have. My parents were encouragers, and the best advice they ever gave me was, don't quit. If you're going to take something on, don't quit. See it through to a logical conclusion and then have the courage to grow. Be willing to expand your mind. Be willing to expand your capacity to understand things that you never thought you would be involved in. My parents were great and spires for me.

turn_text: That's great advice. One final question for my governor. When all said and done, what do you want your legacy to be?

Well, you know, I've never been one of those that thought a lot about a legacy. I think if you do what's right and you confront issues and don't run away from them, I believe that will be the greatest legacy you can have. I do believe, however, that the programs that we put in place during my administration of focusing education on employment, of making sure that children and parents who spend a lot of money getting their children to go to college and get degrees, are going to be an area where jobs are available in Georgia. and that they don't have to leave our state in order to get a job. That keeps families together. It allows grandparents to see their grandchildren when their children have not had to move out of the state. I think my legacy also will be the fact that I have a caring heart. I take on issues that many people say are not important. that they're not politically correct. I was told, when I announced I was going to take on criminal justice reform, that that was a risky thing for a Republican governor to do. My answer was, but it's the right thing to do. If you do the right thing, the politics will take care of itself. That's exactly what's happening. We passed in two separate years major criminal justice reform without a single descending vote in the House of the Senate. The third leg passed with only three descending votes which is virtually a unanimous vote. I believe if you're on the right side of issues that's the best legacy that you can ever have.
